desc: The Air Technical Intelligence Center, established in 1951 out of the Air Materiel Command intelligence organisation (T-2) at Wright Field, was the United States' centre for the exploitation of foreign aerospace technology. It was the organisation that processed the Operation Paperclip haul, that dismantled and reverse-engineered captured Soviet and German airframes, and that was institutionally designed to answer exactly one question: what is this thing and how does it work. Every official UFO project of the legacy era — SIGN, GRUDGE and Blue Book — was hosted here, which is a fact usually reported as an administrative detail and is in fact the central structural point of this domain. The United States did not assign unidentified flying objects to a science agency, an academic body or an air-defence command; it assigned them to the shop that takes recovered hardware apart. The Air Force organizational-history record gives a discontinuation and a new constitution rather than a renaming: the Air Technical Intelligence Center was redesignated Aerospace Technical Intelligence Center on 21 September 1959 and discontinued on 1 July 1961, and the Foreign Technology Division was constituted, activated and organized the same day, absorbing the mission and resources; FTD's own later name is the National Air and Space Intelligence Center, which remains at Wright-Patterson today. It also issued Blue Book Special Report No. 14 in 1955 and was the terminal analytical node under AFR 200-2. If a legacy recovery and exploitation effort existed, ATIC and its successors are the institutional address, and its 1947-1951 T-2 intelligence files have never been subject to a comprehensive declassification review.

dossier.denialPosture: ATIC is not recorded on this board issuing a denial of its own, and its D axis is 0. Its posture is structural rather than spoken: the regulation that named it the analysis authority is the same instrument that governed what could be said publicly, so the centre held the evidence and the parent service held the microphone. That division is worth stating plainly, because it means an absence of ATIC denials is not an absence of denial. The statements this board grades as directed denials in the legacy era are the Air Force's, and they are carried on the usaf node.
dossier.narrative:
Read the regulation rather than the folklore and the placement is explicit. AFR 200-2 of 26 August 1953, paragraph 4a, says that 'The Air Technical Intelligence Center (ATIC), Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, has been designated the Air Force activity responsible for conducting analysis of information and evidence.' The 1954 edition keeps the same terminal position, taking reports from base level through the Air Defense Command and the 4602d Air Intelligence Service Squadron and ending at ATIC.

One correction this board has had to make to its own corpus belongs here, because the mistake is easy and it repeats. The claim that AFR 200-2 routed reports to ATIC rather than to Blue Book is a category error. Project Blue Book was a project inside ATIC at Wright-Patterson; naming ATIC is naming Blue Book's host, and the 1953 regulation does not mention Blue Book at all in either edition.

The second thing the record establishes is that ATIC's analytical work was not confined to reports of things other people saw. TR-AC-47, the joint report on Project Silver Bug of 15 February 1955, carries the Air Technical Intelligence Center imprint on its title page, and its own conclusion asks for direct liaison between WADC and ATIC personnel. That is the same organisation, in the same year it published the largest statistical study of UFO reports the United States has ever produced, working with the Air Force's development command on a circular-planform aircraft.
openQuestions: ATIC's 1947-1951 T-2 intelligence files have never been subject to a comprehensive declassification review. Nothing on this board establishes what is in them.
The 1954 edition of AFR 200-2 is carried here from a transcription at cufon.org rather than from a government scan. The 1953 edition has a four-page image scan behind it; the 1954 one does not.

The board holds no document establishing what ATIC did with any recovered materiel, only that it was the organisation designated to receive and analyse evidence. The custody link through McCoy is graded Tier 2 for that reason.
dossier.whatItIs: The Air Technical Intelligence Center, formed in 1951 out of Air Materiel Command's T-2 intelligence organisation at Wright Field and resident at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. It was the United States' centre for the exploitation of foreign aerospace technology, the shop that processed the Operation Paperclip haul and took captured airframes apart. Every official American UFO project of the legacy era was hosted here: SIGN from 1948, GRUDGE from 1949 and Blue Book from 1952. It issued Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 on 5 May 1955 under Project 10073, Study No. 102-EL-55/2-79, and both editions of AFR 200-2 name it as the Air Force activity responsible for conducting analysis of information and evidence. It became the Foreign Technology Division in 1961 and later the National Air and Space Intelligence Center, which is still at the base.
dossier.whyImplicated: The implicating fact is the assignment, not an allegation. The United States did not send unidentified flying objects to a science agency, to an academic body or to an air-defence command; it sent them to the organisation whose standing function was to answer one question about recovered hardware, which is what it is and how it works. That placement is usually reported as an administrative detail and is the structural point of this whole domain. The board also carries a Tier 2 custody link on the same ground: Howard McCoy ran AMC intelligence from 1945 to 1951, the organisation that received and exploited recovered foreign materiel and that hosted Project SIGN, so any 1947 recovery would have been processed at this address. And ATIC's own 1947-1951 T-2 intelligence files have never been subject to a comprehensive declassification review.
